#4078. GTA 6 Review - An Astounding, Impossible New Bar For Video Games

The most anticipated video game of all time is a triumph on every level that exceeds years of unbelievable expectations. You're not ready for Leonida.

Throughout much of my nearly 100 hours of playtime, reviewing Grand Theft Auto 6 felt like a paradox. Finally getting a chance to see what Rockstar has been cooking for close to a decade is both the most exciting moment of my whole career and the most high-pressure thing I’ve ever been lucky enough to take on. How do you possibly begin to talk about something that had whole studios built just for its NPCs?

GTA 6 is the biggest video game of all time, but we really only knew the basics. Something that dawned on me less than an hour in when it became clear just how much had been held back. Even with the weight of 13 years of anticipation on my shoulders, I’m also well aware that nothing I say about Jason and Lucia’s felonious tour of Leonida will influence the minds of anyone even half interested in it.

The great irony of this herculean task is that, more often than not, Grand Theft Auto 6 left me completely speechless, pointing at the screen and gibbering like an idiot at what Rockstar has accomplished. By every measure, it’s a masterclass of a game that not only lives up to the impossible hype but somehow goes even further by redefining what it means to be a GTA game.

Following the narrative heights of Red Dead Redemption 2 and its beloved Arthur Morgan is an unenviable task, but Grand Theft Auto 6 doesn’t disappoint. It follows Jason and Lucia, two small-time criminals who reunite and are quickly forced to rise through the ranks of Leonida’s underworld after a failed job puts them up against Vice City’s most dangerous forces.

So far, so GTA, but there’s more to the plot than the rags-to-riches setup would have you believe. Unsurprisingly, I can’t tell you much about the overarching story and what sets it in motion, but Jason and Lucia’s involvement has far more emotional and mature stakes than any other game in the series before it. Rockstar takes the pair to places I never would have predicted (including some surprisingly dark moments), and it all lands because of how expertly written and characterised both protagonists are.

Jason is more stoic and guarded than any of the more out-there characters we followed throughout Los Santos, but he’s got a heart of gold and lots of charm underneath the gruff exterior, which mostly comes out when he’s with Lucia. He’s harder to read and takes time to warm up to, but by the end, Jason stands comfortably alongside the series' most memorable protagonists, Niko, CJ, and even Red Dead’s revered gunslingers.

Lucia, on the other hand, is without a doubt the best protagonist in Grand Theft Auto history. She’s fiercely loyal, emotionally mature, witty, and doesn’t take crap from anyone, almost to a fault, as her passion and eagerness to prove herself often land her in trouble. As the series’ first female lead (no, I don’t count the pixel blobs from the first game), there’s a lot of pressure on Lucia, but she easily reaches the lofty bar set by Arthur Morgan.

“We believed in this idea of putting a relationship at the center of the game and trying to make a GTA that was still as funny, crazy, shocking, and fun as the previous games but with added heart. But yeah, the process of making something like this you always question things. As you saw with the 2022 hack, game development isn’t pretty. It can take a long time and a lot of iteration to make good on an idea and to get things working. But I think simply the idea that the relationship would be something that the player needed to work at an earn (or ignore if they want to!) felt like exciting new territory.” - Rupert Humphries, Senior Vice President of Narrative

Of course, as great as Jason and Lucia are on their own merits, they come as a pair in GTA 6 and are together for nearly all of the story’s biggest moments. I had some doubts about the Bonnie and Clyde-style romance, as it's not exactly familiar territory for Rockstar. But after seeing their chemistry and working to give them an unbreakable bond through hand-holding, dates, clubbing, and, of course, doing crime as a pair in my playthrough, I simply can’t imagine the two not being madly in love. Some of my favourite moments in the whole game were simply taking Jason and Lucia on a date, grinning as they flirted, and getting unhealthily invested in their relationship.

It’s not just a win for the story, either, as Jason and Lucia’s cooperative gameplay is a huge step up from GTA 5, with far more options than just swapping, from letting your partner drive you to waypoints and having them cover you in firefights to asking them to fence your stolen goods or hang back as a getaway driver. In GTA 6, having a partner in crime finally means exactly that.

That romance might be the focal point and main standout of GTA 6’s story, but there’s plenty to love about the excellent supporting cast as well. Whether you’re supposed to love them like the cool-as-ice mentor figure Raul or hate them like some characters I won’t dare mention, there’s not a single weak link. Though the writing can occasionally be slightly less biting than previous games, Jason and Lucia’s tale tops GTA 4 as the series’ best narrative.

Perhaps my favourite character of the whole game is Karim, the hacker in Raul’s group who provides some surprising Watch Dogs 2 vibes.

Sony is right - Grand Theft Auto 6 is probably going to play best on PlayStation.

It would have been easy (or at least easier) for Rockstar to take GTA 5’s lucrative formula and just polish the graphics a bit, but one of the biggest strengths of Grand Theft Auto 6 is how it completely rebuilds the main tenets of the whole series. For starters, core mechanics like movement, shooting, and driving all feel far better than ever thanks to extensive improvements and tweaks.

Take GTA’s infamous mash X to sprint controls, for instance, which have been completely reworked for a more standardised and smoother experience. Jason and Lucia are both far more agile than previous protagonists and have more vertical options at every moment, which makes the simple act of getting around on foot much more enjoyable. The only downside to the rework, and spoilers for the rest of this review - the game as a whole - is that the controls can sometimes be a little overcomplicated due to how many interactions you have at your disposal.

It did take me a good few hours to adjust to the new control scheme, but it’ll be incredibly tough to go back now. There is an option for the classic version if you really struggle, though.

“There was lot a lot of internal team feedback to look at our controls and responsiveness after we launched RDR2, so we doubled down on exploring an ‘experimental’ control scheme as it was called internally at the time. The experiment kind of stalled mid development due to other competing priorities but was revitalized by Rob (Head of Development). After that, we all strongly felt it should be the default control scheme as we’d had consistently good feedback from the team and user research. We still offer classic GTA controls in the setting menu for those prefer them. Indeed, we have many people at R* who still do! There are also a lot more options for players to explore in the menu. Hopefully, there is a scheme or set of options for everyone to enjoy the game!” - David Hynd, Vice President of Technology

Shooting, meanwhile, takes cues from Red Dead Redemption 2 and its weightier weapons, which already felt inspired by Max Payne 3’s stellar gunfights. There’s even a Dead Eye/Bullet Time slow-motion focus mode for both protagonists, rather than being locked as a special ability for one character, and it becomes an essential tool as you go up against the gangs and cops of Leonida. It’s the best combat has ever felt in a Grand Theft Auto game by a country mile.

The same goes for driving, which sits somewhere between GTA 5 and GTA 4 thanks to a greater focus on vehicle weight, physics, and damage while somehow still retaining the buttery smooth controls and flow. Driving is also the most immediately obvious example of Rockstar not just improving how Grand Theft Auto 6 plays, but recontextualising every mechanic’s implementation with a greater focus on worldbuilding and player involvement.

Unlike previous games in the series where you could grab a fast car and bomb it down the city streets without so much as tapping the brakes, Leonida’s denser traffic and narrower streets (including a ton of painfully realistic roadworks) mean you need to be paying attention at all times. It’s only when you start to master the new systems and put the effort in that you can weave through traffic like a pro, which makes it infinitely more rewarding. Couple that with cars requiring far more work to attain thanks to higher security and a ridiculous amount of upgrade and modding options, and vehicles become so much more than just something you steal, park in your garage, and don’t give a second thought to.

On the other hand, gunfights are no longer about just aiming for the head with whatever arsenal you’ve got in your back pocket, as you now need to incapacitate enemies with clean, targeted shots to the knees and arms if you want to keep a professional criminal profile. You also have a more limited choice of weapons, forcing you to plan ahead and keep your trunk stocked before a firefight. Even crime, the main thing Grand Theft Auto is known for, is completely different in GTA 6. Not only are the police more advanced than ever before, with multiple stages of realistic awareness of your actions that incentivise masks, stealth, and being as efficient as possible, but there’s far more effort that needs to be put in for even the simplest of sins.

"A lot of work, yeah! There were a few key areas we needed to change for cops in particular on this game. The perception/recognition system needed a complete overhaul. On V/RDR the cops always knew where the player was located, but with the new model they now rely on proper search/investigation routines, guided by witness reports and evidence (e.g. dead bodies, abandoned vehicles). K9 units can sense the player too, so you need to keep on your toes when they are around! And, of course, we added appearance and outfit recognition to add depth/roleplay mechanics to cop evasion. Having an unknown wanted state created lots of great gameplay moments, where you could nonchalantly leave a crime scene undetected. And adding in Heat added a level of persistence that was lacking in previous games. The wanted UI also took a lot of time to finesse/balance. We added threat indicators to give the player more feedback around how they were being perceived by cops/enemies in game. This opened up some cool stealth gameplay opportunities, but was also crucial seeing as we removed enemies from the radar. Once you are spotted, we now rely on cops calling it in before you fully known. This gives the player a window of opportunity to deal with the situation before things kick off.  But yeah, it’s been a massive effort. Fueled by constant tweaks and iteration over many years." - David Hynd, Vice President of Technology

Gone are the days of completing a few story missions and having millions in the bank without anything to spend it on, as money is incredibly hard to come by in Vice City. You really need to work for it, whether through simple but low-reward gas station stick-ups and jewel store heists, or storming gang hideouts for drugs you can sell on to fences. What’s most impressive about all of the crime opportunities is that they’re completely emergent and up to the player, a massive leap forward from Los Santos story-specific heists and very basic convenience store shakedowns.

As if being able to pull off story mission-esque heists at any moment wasn’t enough, GTA 6 has also made some notable improvements to the main campaign. When they’re not trying to make Jason and Lucia feel like real people with quieter moments, story missions are energetic, bombastic, and, unlike some criticisms of Red Dead Redemption 2, give the player more freedom and control than before. While I’m sure some players will prefer the classic, more thoughtless approach, for my money Grand Theft Auto 6 is a better and more considered game on every single front, pushing the series formula to impossible new heights.

In a game that’s all triumphs, the biggest of all is Grand Theft Auto 6’s meticulously crafted world, which is so unbelievably impressive it single-handedly justifies the long wait. From the murky swamps near Leonida Keys to the neon-lit upper echelons of Capri, Leonida is jaw-dropping at every turn (fittingly for Vice City, especially at night) and a downright feat of engineering to get it all working without any issues on PS5 Pro. Some things, especially the weather system and frankly ridiculous lighting, need to be seen to be believed.

I’ve never stopped to smell the roses so much in a game, but it’s impossible not to soak in all of the work and love that’s gone into every explorable interior, every beach packed with NPCs you can interact with or just hear have detailed conversations, every neighbourhood with potential things to steal, and every flea market with functioning shops. Almost all of the effort feels necessary to deliver on the promise of Leonida, but you can often feel Rockstar flexing its penchant for the little details (such as food being realistically eaten and the unique games that are playable on the PlayStation parody) that make these worlds feel so real.

Grand Theft Auto 6 also easily has the best radio selection the series has seen since Vice City. Justice’s original soundtrack is also incredible and punctuates major story moments perfectly.

Rockstar’s foray into heightened realism in Red Dead Redemption 2 has clearly left its mark on GTA 6, which focuses heavily on immersion and realism. You can shower, work out at the gym to build muscle, eat food to put on weight, get tired from not sleeping enough, need to keep vehicles filled with fuel, and have more hairstyle and clothing options than you know what to do with. I was a little worried it’d go too far and end up a little intense like RDR2, but Rockstar has taken the right amount of inspiration from that game while still making sure GTA isn’t getting too close to a life-sim.

“I personally love going into a gas station, buying a hot dog and a slushie and walking out alternating between eating and drinking and walking down the street doing that, then throwing the empty cup in the trash. I love getting a six pack of beers and walking along drinking them one at a time, throwing them around!”- Rob Nelson, Head of Development

Beyond being so detailed and immersive, Leonida is also just an incredibly varied and handcrafted county that feels unique no matter where you go. It’s a far cry from GTA 5’s handful of city areas mixed with vast wilderness that ends up getting ignored, and it helps that it’s stuffed with side missions, minigames, and emergent events that keep the water-cooler spirit Rockstar’s games are so well known for.

It might feel like I’ve said a lot about GTA 6 (it certainly does to me, anyway), but even with close to 100 hours, there are still whole areas I’ve barely explored, mechanics I’ve only glanced at, easter eggs to find, and activities that are begging for more of my time - it’s an absolute juggernaut. There’s also so much I can’t talk about or simply don’t want to get into to keep the sense of discovery for everyone else.

Without a shadow of a doubt, Grand Theft Auto 6 is the best open-world game I’ve ever played, and one of the best games full stop, with only incredibly minute nitpicks barely worth mentioning that do nothing to drag it down from masterpiece status. Its jaw-droppingly detailed world, completely revamped and recontextualised mechanics, and heartfelt narrative with two stellar leads put it far above the rest of the incredible series and set an impossible new bar for the medium as a whole. I'm sure we’ll never see another game with such unreal hype that actually lives up to and exceeds expectations, but you can rest easy knowing that the long road to Leonida was worth walking.

We finally got a chance to play The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake and it's still one of the best games ever made.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#4077. Marathon launch player numbers are about half those of the Server Slam, at least on PC

Marathon hasn't quite been able to attract the same volume of players the recent Server Slam did.

After a couple of delays, a plagiarism lawsuit, and at least one internal reboot, Bungie’s next big game has officially launched. Marathon, the extraction shooter from the studio behind Destiny, has managed to find a decent, if a little small of an audience.

The game’s player numbers on Steam are being compared to its recent free, open weekend, and not in a favourable manner.

Prior to Marathon’s launch, Bungie held a multi-day Server Slam, which offered anyone interested in playing the game a chance to try out almost all of its classes, two of its maps, as well as many of its gameplay and progression systems.

The open test was largely well-received, and players actually showed up for it. It peaked at a very respectable 143,621 concurrent players on Steam, which put it within striking distance of the peak concurrent of its chief competitor, Arc Raiders - at least when you compare both of their pre-launch Server Slam events.

In Arc Raiders’ case, those figures were far outpaced at the game’s actual launch, and the Embark shooter continues to command a very active player base to this day. A paid product garnering far more players than the same product’s own free sampler is never not a good sign, so many hoped something similar would happen with Marathon.

Marathon has now officially launched, and it doesn’t look like it managed to pull an Arc Raiders - at least so far. At its peak, the Bungie shooter attracted 88,337 concurrent players on Steam (via SteamDB), which is a little over half of its Server Slam’s 143,621 peak concurrent.

Numbers have, of course, dropped since then, which is normal, as players log off for the night. This is obviously not the end of the road for Marathon. Friday, and the weekend, may well push numbers closer to the Server Slam heights.

Indeed, word of mouth is quite positive, with the game currently sitting at a Very Positive user review rating on Steam, based on over 4,600 reviews. As has been proven time and time again in recent years, nothing catapults a game like players emphatically advocating for it to their friends, so it could simply be that mainstream players are cautious.

It will become clear where things settle over the weekend.

#4076. Marvel 1943: Rise Of Hydra Reportedly Still In Development Amid Rumors Of Its Cancellation

Yesterday, a rumor emerged on X claiming that Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra, the upcoming World War II-era superhero game led by Uncharted creator Amy Hennig, was being cancelled. After making the rounds on social media, new reports claim this is not the case, at least for now.

The rumor stemmed from a now-deleted X post from a fan account called Marvel 1943 Rise Of Hydra Countdown claiming, through supposed inside sources, that Skydance was preparing to announce the game’s cancellation. This rumor was quickly picked up and circulated by online gaming circles, gaining steam due to growing uncertainty around the game’s status.

Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra was revealed in 2022 and stars Captain America and Black Panther (Azurri, T'Challa's grandfather), alongside Howling Commandos member Gabriel Jones and Wakandan Spy Network leader Nanali, as they battle Hydra during World War II. Developed by Skydance New Media, led by Amy Hennig, it’s been repeatedly delayed, and only cinematic footage has been released. This has understandably caused many to question the game’s fate.

However, a few hours after the cancellation rumor made the rounds, Bloomberg’s Jason Schreier reported on Bluesky that Skydance’s leadership addressed the rumor with the development team on Slack and assured them Marvel 1943 was not canceled. However, Schreier adds this could change due to the uncertainty caused by the recent merger between Warner Bros. Discovery and Paramount Skydance (Skydance New Media is a game development branch of the now-merged Skydance Corporation).

Skydance Games told the development team behind Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra on Slack this afternoon that the game is not canceled, despite a widely circulated rumor on Twitter today claiming that it was.

Furthermore, Kotaku’s Rebekah Valentine clarified in her report that Marvel 1943 executive producer Lu Giglotti told staff in a Skydance Slack message he’d spoken directly with the executive leadership team to confirm Marvel 1943 is still alive, saying, "There is no truth to these claims." According to Kotaku’s report, Giglotti informed the team that Marvel 1943 was approaching an Alpha milestone later this month. Giglotti also told staff not to let the rumor distract them and that Skydance was "monitoring the situation" to address in the future.

Kotaku’s report also sheds light on the game’s tumultuous development cycle. Marvel 1943 was originally pitched as a Netflix game before it was eventually turned into a console and PC title. This transition means the current iteration is “light on gameplay” and lacks substantial interactions, with players primarily using a single button to play it.

This isn't a completely surprising revelation, as Marvel 1943 was billed as a narrative-driven, linear single-player experience when it was revealed, but the style of game has never been clear. The same reveal also saw Skydance promise the game boasted "intuitive controls and exhilarating second-to-second gameplay that captures the action and excitement of Marvel, inspired by landmark comics, television, and films, as they navigate this all-new globe-trotting adventure." This disconnect may be attributed to Kotaku also reporting that Marvel 1943 is “well over budget,” and its overall scope has been heavily scaled back. Regardless, the outlet’s source claims the game is “close to done.”

Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra was initially slated to launch in 2025. It was then delayed to early 2026 "to add more polish", according to Skydance, before being pushed again to an undetermined launch window. The game has no announced platforms.

Although Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra appears safe for now, other recent projects have not been as fortunate. Be sure to read our stories about the recent high-profile cancellations of Gang of Dragon and Fairgames.

#4075. Ocarina Of Time, Pokopia, Fire Emblem & More Pick Up The Game Awards 2026 Nominations

We are rapidly approaching the arrival of The Game Awards on 10th December, and today, Geoff Keighley has announced all of the nominees for this year's show.

While the weight of GTA 6 cast its shadow over most categories (come on, it's not even out yet!), Nintendo picked up a good number of nominations itself, including a spot in the all-important GOTY top six for Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Heck, it's the most-nominated publisher this year with 12 nods all to itself — overtaking the likes of Capcom (11), Annapurna Interactive (9) and PlayStation (9)

Link's latest is joined by 007 First Light, Control Resonant, Grand Theft Auto 6, Phantom Blade 0 and Resident Evil Requiem in the running for this year's top prize.

Here are all of the Nintendo games that have been nominated for the 2026 show, accompanied by the categories in which they'll appear:

On the Nintendo-related side of things, Switch 2 exclusive Orbitals picked up nominations in the Best Multiplayer Game and Best Debut Game categories, and The Super Mario Galaxy Movie is nominated for the Best Adaptation Award.

You'll find the full list of this year's nominees on The Game Awards' website. The full awards show will be livestreamed on YouTube on 10th December.

Do you reckon Nintendo will take home any of the above awards? Who will win GOTY? Let us know in the comments.

#4074. Nioh 3 patch finally makes summons useful in boss fights, brings free armour for everyone

There's a new Nioh 3 patch out in the wild, and it's one that any player who regularly summons in boss fights will really appreciate.

Team Ninja continues to work on Nioh 3. The developer has been releasing regular updates for the action RPG since its launch in early February. Earlier patches have addressed major bugs like healing item use inconsistencies, and more have arrived since to tackle various balance and loot-related issues.

Today’s patch, version 1.04, is a major one, coming in at well over 1GB. There’s plenty here worth getting excited about, so let’s dig in.

To begin with, this is the patch that adds the promised free armour sets for both Ninja, and Samurai. When Nioh 3 reached one million sales, Team Ninja said it would gift every player the Thunderous set in celebration, and the set’s two variants are now available in-game.

The more interesting side of the patch is, unsurprisingly, its change log. There appears to be a focus on online co-op and AI summons in this one, with various tweaks to the make the process more rewarding, and, in some cases, worthwhile.

The amount of Glory obtained when you complete a mission in multiplayer has been increased, regardless of which player was the host. The other major change mainly affects AI Benevolent Grave summons, making it so bosses will no longer target a single player for almost the entirety of the fight.

While summoning AI helpers has always been useful in Nioh 3, they didn’t always help in boss fights, specifically because the boss tended to focus on the player who summoned them, leaving the AI to run around eating AoE hits before dying.

Patch 1.04 makes a couple of welcome gameplay tweaks to the feel of combat. Ninjutsu, and Onmyo Magic will now hit their targets more consistently in situations where there’s a difference in elevation between the player and the enemy.

In the same vein, you’ll now be able to attack (quick/strong) right after jumping, which removes the pause that previously buffered the attack instead. This could mean even more air combos that don’t specifically require Martial Arts.

You can look forward to a couple of quality of life tweaks in this patch, too, such as the change that allows the game to automatically send any Sudama Soul Cores dropped by merchants to your item box. This happens from the second one onwards, which means you won’t have to pick half a dozen each time you go to sell a batch of items.

Speaking of the item box, the limit of forging materials has been increased for some of them. If you’ve been running Battle Scroll missions and Expeditions for gear, you’ll be happy to know that you can now exit the session from the main menu directly.

There’s plenty more to patch 1.04, including fixes and balance tweaks for several weapons, such as Samurai dual swords, odachi, and more for a few Ninja weapons, too. The patch also brings several bug fixes to the game.

You can read the full set of patch notes on Steam.

#4073. Guide: GTA 6 Release Times: All The Key Details Xbox Players Need To Know

It's finally here! We've officially reached the launch week of GTA 6 on Xbox Series X, Xbox Series S, PS5 and even the Xbox One (kind of), 13 long years since the most recent entry in the series back in 2013.

With that in mind, we thought we'd put up a quick release times guide so you know exactly when you can start playing the game, and we've also thrown in a few extra details about what we're expecting for Xbox One players at launch.

So, here are all the deets you need to know for Thursday!

On this page: GTA 6 Release Times: All The Key Details Xbox Players Need To Know

The official GTA 6 release date is Thursday, November 19th. You may still see people playing it on Wednesday though, as depending on where you live, certain players will be getting access to it earlier than others.

GTA 6 releases at midnight local time around the world. This means you'll be able to start playing it on Xbox Series X, Xbox Series S and PS5 as soon as November 18th turns into November 19th in your region.

The only exception to the rule may be in countries with multiple time zones. For example, Rockstar seems to be classing "midnight" based around the EST time zone in the US, which would mean PST gets it at 9pm on the 18th.

Technically, yes. Due to the staggered rollout, players in New Zealand will be getting first access to GTA 6 at midnight in their time zone, which equates to 11am on November 18th here in the UK, and even earlier in the United States.

We urge caution around this, as Xbox's terms of service specifically state that you shouldn't switch regions unless you're actually located in the country you're switching to, but we'll leave the decision up to you.

News Xbox Fans Urge Caution Over New Zealand Trick For GTA 6, While Others Say It's A Non-Issue

"They literally told me this in person in Seattle at Xbox FanFest last week"

You may have noticed that we didn't mention Xbox One in the release times section up above, and that's because we don't quite know what's happening with it. In a nutshell, Xbox One players will be forced to use Xbox Cloud Gaming in order to get access to GTA 6, which in theory should require buying the game before access is granted.

There are too many unknowns ahead of launch about how this works though. Will cloud access be made available immediately? Will you be able to use the free-with-ads version of the cloud to play GTA 6, or will it require paying for the service? Is it just Xbox One that you can play it on, or will mobile and PC devices be supported too?

That's where we stand ahead of launch, so while GTA 6 definitely will be playable through the cloud on Xbox One in some form, it's probably best to wait until it's been released before handing over any money as things stand.

Rockstar also confirms GTA 6 will run at 30FPS

Of course, we've already talked about the preload for GTA 6 and how anyone can download the game right now on Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S, regardless of whether they've actually bought it or not.

All that's left is to wait a few more days until the new Grand Theft Auto finally becomes available, and we can't wait to see whether it'll live up to the hype and become a Game of the Year contender when it arrives this Thursday.

#4071. The Sims 4 patch makes it so your public lot gatherings won't be interrupted by rogue Sims

Stranger Sims will no longer just crash your public lot events in The Sims 4 to talk about whatever.

The Sims 4 will soon get a new update to resolve a number of issues, some of which have long caused headaches for players. The latest update will arrive March 17 on PC and Mac, followed by PlayStation and Xbox at an unspecified time later.

Outside of the fixes themselves, the patch also makes good on the recent re-commitment to continue improving quality of life for players, so there’s plenty here longtime players will appreciate.

In the latest episode of The Sims 4’s Laundry List blog series, where the developer goes through the most reported problems with the game and how it plans to solve them, we got a rundown of what to expect from next week’s patch.

You can look forward to five major fixes in this one, but arguably the most important is a change to how Sims determine who they speak with on a lot. This is especially relevant for public lots, where Sims would sometimes interrupt ongoing conversations by barging in and starting a conversation with your Sim.

Going forward, Sims will prioritise familiar Sims with whom they already have rapport, and be less likely to latch onto strangers. If you’ve witnessed a date your Sim was on get interrupted because of that, you’ll certainly appreciate the change.

Speaking of budding romance, Prom is coming back to in-game Calendars, and Sims can once again attend. Maxis said this will work with new and existing saves, and that you should also expect Prom goals to be completable once again.

Pets and animals get some love in this patch, too. First, pets and horses will no longer get lost in Premade Households. The fix prevents that from happening in new saves, but if you already had that happen to you in your current save, it’ll still be there.

You may now also assign animals to an Animal Shed after moving your house to a new lot, so you hopefully won’t be confused as to why they’re stuck in your inventory. This fix applies to existing saves as well as new ones.

Lower down the list of urgent fixes is an update that makes it so Sims’ eye blinking will show fully closed eyes for most interactions. The upcoming patch also comes with a host of Sims autonomy fixes, including one that prevents them from excessively flirting with each other.

Catch up on the full list at the link near the top of the page. And, in case you missed it, Maxis recently announced that The Sims 4 will soon get paid mods, something that many in the community are skeptical about.

#4068. Crimson Desert PC specs don't keep resolution and framerate targets a secret, and they don't use upscaling for everything either

Finally, a PC specification list that actually indicates resolution and framerate targets, and doesn't leave console players behind.

Crimson Desert is a little over one week away from release, and developer Pearl Abyss has delivered the official, final list of specs for the game. The twist is that the specs not only include useful information for PC players, they also cover similarly relevant details for console players, who traditionally don’t get mentioned in those reveals.

The specs are decently detailed, but more surprisingly - except for a single instance - they don’t include upscaling on PC, another thing games have gotten too comfortable using, even with their lowest specs.

On the official Crimson Desert website, developer Pearl Abyss has delivered a chunky post breaking down five different sets of PC requirements for the upcoming open-world action RPG. Each set indicates the graphics preset being used - and crucially, the resolution and framerate targets you can expect with each.

With the exception of the Minimum spec, all other presets do not appear to rely on upscaling of any kind. They do not say, however, whether ray tracing is being used with any of them, which is a feature that will throw all of those specs out of whack.

That same transparency also extends to non-PC platforms, which traditionally get few, if any, details about their own resolution and framerate targets. The console set of specs are extensive, just like PC, covering both PlayStation, and Xbox.

It’s granular enough to indicate which upscaling tech is being used, where applicable. This is relevant for owners of a PS5 Pro, a console that has access to Sony’s PSSR upscaling, alongside the standard AMD FSR tech the base console - and Xbox - use.

The developer has also revealed the base resolution for each mode across each console, and the resolution the image will be upscaled to using whichever tech is being utilised.

And, if you’re one of the five people who play games on Mac, you’ll be thrilled to know that the specs also include a section for Mac devices, split between the different Mac chips. The quality preset being used with each is not clear, however.

Finally, there's a set of specs for the Rog Xbox Ally, covering both the X and S models.

Crimson Desert arrives March 20 on PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S. You can expect more coverage from us at release and beyond.

#4067. God Of War Sons Of Sparta Gets PS4 Version And New Content Next Monday

It's been about nine months since Sony Santa Monica and Mega Cat Studios dropped God of War Sons of Sparta as a surprise reveal and launch during a State of Play. If you haven't checked it out yet, the developers are giving you some new reasons to today, unveiling two new modes and a new platform: PlayStation 4.

If you don't remember, God of War Sons of Sparta is a prequel spin-off of the God of War series, showing protagonist Kratos as a 13-year-old soldier, long before his god-killing days. The game features 2D combat and a Metroidvania-style map, along with a fully voiced cast of characters including Scott Menville (who you might recognize as Robin in Teen Titans) as Kratos' brother Deimos, Jack Quaid (who will voice a different character in God of War Laufey next year), and TC Carson, who returns from the original trilogy as the voice of adult Kratos.

Announced in a post on the PlayStation Blog today, Sons of Sparta is making the jump back to Sony's previous console, which is now (brace yourself) 13 years old. Sons of Sparta's 2D pixel art is far less demanding than the other God of War entries, though, so it's no surprise this was possible – it's mainly surprising that they're doing it at all.

For PS5 players who already own the game, developer Mega Cat is also adding two new modes: Hermes Mode and Erebus Mode. Hermes Mode, named after the Greek god of wind, mail, and speed, is a speedrun mode that encourages you to beat the game as quickly as possible, complete with a split-based timer in the upper right-hand corner of the screen. Meanwhile, Erebus Mode, named after one of the domains of the underworld (you'll be familiar with it if you've played the Hades games), makes the game far deadlier as Kratos and all his foes die in a single hit. You'll have to wait until you beat the game once to unlock Erebus Mode, but you can access Hermes Mode from a fresh save by entering the following (and semi-familiar) code in the start menu: Up, Up, Down, Down, Left, Right, Left, Right, L1, R1, Touchpad.

The free update and PS4 version will be available next Monday, November 16, at midnight local time. For more Sons of Sparta, check out our review. For more God of War, bad news: God of War Laufey was just delayed until May.

#4066. Talking Point: As A Parent, What Worries You Most About Gaming?

Nintendo's guide aims to highlight the benefits

Over the summer, I replayed Ocarina of Time (1998) with my kids. I hadn't intended to, but it dawned on me that once the gorgeous remake landed, the original's visible polygons might not hold the same appeal for them. It was selfish, really, but I wanted them to experience the original magic as I did.

I held the pad but let them direct me, staying silent or feigning ignorance about puzzle solutions, letting them speculate and point out chests and switches I'd intentionally run past, involving them in an adventure they don't quite have the dexterity to control themselves.

I worried their attention might wander while watching for 30-60 minutes at a time, and I don't want to be that parent, forcing something I loved on my disinterested kids ("What do you mean 'Thunderbirds is boring'?!"). I was ready to pull the cord if they didn't take to it.

But no! They were pointing and problem-solving alongside me, jumping up and down, utterly engaged and loving the story and our shared experience.

Beyond the screen, Ocarina provoked laughter over dinner, and discussion about why characters reacted as they did, the cause and effect of actions, and the resulting emotions. Car journeys suddenly had a new soundtrack accompaniment, and the game's themes would come up while drawing or playing with Lego or finding a 'Deku' stick out on a walk. It became a rich source of inspiration for their imaginations, and a springboard to conversation and closeness with my kids. A fantastic family adventure we'll remember for years to come.

It's such a shame, then, when you see parents whose kids love games struggle to recognise the benefits and sheer joy they can bring, and potentially miss out on family experiences like mine. For something so ubiquitous and so fun, gaming can create real tension in the home and throw up generational barriers that take time and understanding to break down.

And with all the online concerns and other ills of the modern age, it's easy to see why some parents might perceive games as a dead-end, dangerous time sink that needs to be contained and quarantined, like fast food or social media.

According to a recent Ofcom report, 88% of children aged 3-17 in the UK play games on some form of device, and given Nintendo's evergreen, all-ages remit to deliver surprise and delight, addressing concerns of gaming-cautious guardians is something the company is keen on, beyond the bare minimum of secure account systems and Parental Control tools.

So that'll be why they've partnered up with Andy Robertson, founder of the Family Gaming Database and longtime friend of the site, for the recently published Parent's Guide to Gaming with Confidence.

Longtime Nintendo Life readers may recognise Andy from the various articles and reviews he's penned for us over the years, or from our partnership with Family Gaming to highlight accessibility information in our reviews and game pages across the network.

Produced in association with Nintendo, in this new guide Andy has also enlisted other experts in the fields of gaming, child psychology, and online safety to help parents of all gaming backgrounds digest the key questions and perhaps reframe how some of them view video games.

The prevalence of online gaming and voice chat worries me a lot. I don't want my kid speaking to strangers or picking up bad language or habits. Everything is so much easier (and tempting) to access than it used to be!

Available as a downloadable PDF, Andy explores common misconceptions and offers sound advice from expert contributors, including child psychologist Dr Amanda Gummer and Dr Catherine Knibbs, a child and adult psychotherapist specialising in online harm.

As you'll see from the breakout boxes on this page, uncertainties about other online players and predatory monetisation systems are the main sources of anxiety for NL staff with kids. "I'm very concerned about exploitative mechanics," says Alex, our senior video producer, "things designed to get their hooks into people's brains and make them dependent, or cough up wads of cash."

According to Ofcom's research, these are common worries:

The biggest type of concern among parents and carers of 3-17-year-olds who play games online is their child talking to strangers through games or via the chat functions (64%). This is followed by concerns about bullying by other players (60%), exposure to inappropriate content such as violence, bad language or disturbing material (59%), and pressure to make in-game purchases (51%).

Dr Knibbs highlights how "digital spaces can feel less familiar" than physical play spaces like playgrounds. The dangers can be less obvious, too, although she stresses that understanding the risks is better than avoidance. "When we learn about the content, the people and the spaces our children are engaging with, we are much better placed to help them navigate those experiences safely and positively."

It's not just about risk assessment, but also realising the potential benefits - and that doesn't require extensive gaming experience. "The goal ISN’T to become a gamer," Andy writes. "It is to better understand the people you care about most." You don't need to have conquered Elden Ring or any other game to participate and 'get' games.

Games with random or chance-based outcomes, especially with microtransactions that encourage you to spend money and try again, are what concern me most. As much as I enjoy it, Pokémon GO is a strong example of this (there’s a reason it was recently bumped up to PEGI 16), but thankfully, there are enough single-player adventures out there (Pokémon included!) that can minimise these often frustrating and FOMO-driven elements for younger players.

Another key point to stress to non-gaming parents might seem almost self-evident, but it's easily overlooked if recognising Mario and Pac-Man represents your sum knowledge of the medium.

For some, even now, 'gaming' remains an arcade-style competition for high scores, and that can create a disconnect between parents with preconceived notions and their kids, who are discovering that games can be so much more.

"A child who is creating, collaborating, problem-solving or connecting with friends is having a very different experience from someone passively consuming content," Dr Amanda Gummer writes in a section of the guide highlighting "one of the most common mistakes parents make" - that all games are essentially the same.

We can all recall 'Wow, games can do this???' moments when the scales fell from our eye. It might have been an emotional beat in Shadow of the Colossus, or a surprising Wii Sports session with grandparents over the holidays; whatever the source, getting the uninitiated to that point is a crucial first step. While it's all notionally 'reading', hopping between Wikipedia articles is obviously not the same as reading a poem or sitting down with James Patterson's latest or doomscrolling social media feeds or taking a crack at Ulysses, and once parents understand that the world of video games is equally expansive, they've got a foundation to build upon.

Andy takes time to break down what he terms "the myth of the isolated gamer" and how, in fact, games can bring families together. Living the Nintendo life as we do, multiplayer has been commonplace for decades, but the lone gamer in the basement/attic stereotype persists.

Likewise — and this has long been a personal bugbear when talking with friends and family — rationing 'screen time' feels like an oversimplification for parents guarding against passive media consumption. Lamenting how young people these days don't get enough fresh air is absolutely valid, and getting out in the park, playground, and beyond is crucial to a child's overall development, but it's not as simple as 'outside=good, inside=bad'. The storytelling, learning, collaboration, creativity, and deep experiences games can offer are enormously valuable.

As Andy points out, "understanding the quality of the experience is often more useful than simply counting the minutes." Bowling in Switch Sports, having the national news on in the background, diving into a Mario world, and throwing Bluey on Disney+ are all different types of 'screen time', each with their own benefits and potential drawbacks.

You may not have noticed, but Nintendo Life has grown recently. Behind the scenes, we've had new additions to the family, with two team members recently joining the ranks of Hookshot Media parentdom.

Across our editorial, video, and management teams, our collective tribe runs the age gamut from newborn to undergrad, so we've got a broad range of experience, making it fairly simple to gauge what's appropriate for our kids, suggest games they might like (or slyly leave them lying around to be 'discovered') while monitoring interactions and steering them towards the all-timers (hi, Ocarina) and, importantly, away from less healthy, obsessive patterns that we may have fallen into in our youth.

And yes, there are certain games, primarily targeting younger gamers, that we wouldn't install on any device in the house.

I don’t worry too much about microtransactions as I will maintain strict control over any potential in-game purchases. However, I dread the day that my daughter gets roped into playing something like Roblox. Substantial, well-made games can offer a lot of value for children, but Roblox is not an example of this.

Authorities in some territories are taking steps to mitigate the potential harm of the aggressive monetisation systems baked into platforms like Roblox. In the last week, the EU published its Digital Fairness Act proposal, which could impact any game featuring in-game purchases in the EU. Among other things, the bloc is seeking to curtail "addictive design", "dark patterns", and predatory monetisation tactics.

The DFA would only affect players in Europe, but regulation that forces real currency prices and lootbox odds to be displayed, those and similar systems defaulting to 'off' for minors, and parental consent being required to activate them are all positive steps.

While legislation could mean big changes for some developers and publishers, it's unlikely to cause Nintendo itself headaches.

With first-party software, in-game purchases are typically limited to DLC expansions or Switch 2 Upgrade Packs, and content-wise, it's a rare Nintendo game that I wouldn't feel comfortable playing with my kids in the room - something our teams over on Push Square and Pure Xbox have to be more cautious about, I'd wager.

My child is too young to play games on their own yet, but we’re having a blast with Mario Kart World’s Free Roam mode. It’s perfect, honestly: beyond the vibrant, fun characters, and chancing upon helicopters, lorries, and UFOs you can play as, seeing them gradually understand the geography of this vast world as you string one P-Switch mission to the next has made one of my favourite ever Mario Kart (and gaming) experiences.

Every kid is different, of course. Some may not be phased at all by a lurching ReDead in Hyrule Castle Town, while others might be kept up at night after glimpsing a creepy icon on the home screen. Handily, Switch's handheld hybrid format does make it easier to take the game away from the living room if, say, you need half an hour with Resident Evil Requiem away from eager eyes, and the console's aforementioned Parental Controls and accompanying app make monitoring the kids' gaming pretty simple.

Communicating to nervous parents not just the risks but the rewards is something we're passionate about on the team, and that's something that Andy's guide does particularly well. "Failure is a part of success," he writes. "Games create safe environments where mistakes are expected. This can help children build resilience without even realising it. Every setback becomes part of learning." Makes me feel better about all the times the dogs got me in Call of Duty.

Gaming with an infant is… difficult! (Try explaining that Fortune's Weave isn't touchscreen to a five-month-old). But I genuinely can't wait until my child is old enough to participate; as cheesy as it is, I think I'm going to well up when she picks her first starter Pokémon.

Confidence is a key term. Naturally, it's in Nintendo's interest to maintain its carefully curated family-friendly image, but giving parents who aren't embedded in the ins and outs of the gaming scene the confidence to engage is a win for the medium and everyone who loves it. A digestible guide like this for game-sceptic family and friends could come in handy over the holidays.

(To be clear, I'm not advocating becoming a gaming missionary at the dinner table and forcing pamphlets on relatives. But, you know, slyly leaving them lying around to be 'discovered' and having Switch Sports Resort ready to go after dessert? A round of golf and some bowling has worked wonders in the past!)

As with anything, a good grasp of the issues is essential, and every parent and child will have their own approaches, preferences, and ideas. For the NL team, though — and for me personally — sharing how games can enrich our family lives regardless of experience and ability is important. By alleviating concerns and highlighting benefits, we can open doors for new players and experience more of those treasured 'Oh, games can do this???' moments together.

What worries you most as a parent? Which games have you played and enjoyed the most with your kids? Let us know your thoughts in the polls below, and feel free to take to the comments to share your experiences and the effect gaming has in your family.

My biggest concerns with them and gaming for younger audiences in general are the predatory nature of the games and the lack of concern for their safety from almost all involved parties.

The first point is simple: from what I’ve seen, games on Roblox are meant to be as addictive as possible. By getting kids hooked, they’ll want to keep coming back for more. They do this by having instant feedback loops where you feel like you’re accomplishing something great by ticking up a number constantly. And by implementing the cosmetics and currencies, they’ll be tempted to ask for money for Robux. It just feels predatory.

The last part is on the games, but also on parents. I don’t want to say my siblings are not parenting well, but they’re not gamers, so to me, they don’t seem to be monitoring what their kids consume. And Roblox, as we’ve heard in recent news, can be a breeding ground for predators. It feels way too easy for kids to have access to people they can chat with, and unless a parent is actively monitoring every person they chat to, they don’t know if the person on the other end has good motives.

I don’t want to act like online gaming can’t be helpful for kids, and honestly, kids should be able to play online with their friends. But I think it requires a lot more vigilance from their parents. Long gone are the days where an iPad could babysit a kid (a practice I didn’t even like back when iPads were first introduced). As the father of a four-year-old girl and a one-year-old boy, I care deeply about teaching my children never to become blindly loyal to any brand—not even when it comes to something as personal and entertaining as video games.

I want them to understand the importance of maintaining their bargaining power as consumers and never becoming easy targets of marketing campaigns, whether obvious or subtle, designed to trigger emotional responses and drive impulse purchases.

Just because they may grow up enjoying a privileged lifestyle doesn't mean they should buy things without stopping to consider what those products are actually worth. That kind of judgment requires reason, not emotion.

This doesn't mean raising them to be cold or detached people. Quite the opposite: I want them to be loving, warm, and fun. But when it comes to consuming, I want them to be rational, independent, and deliberate.

Our family didn't get to where it is by spending money carelessly, and I want my children to understand that.

I don't worry so much, but I am very aware of my kids being able to find a solution. Games are really good for showing them a specific context and a problem, then asking them to solve that in order to move forward, and that is very much life itself. Gaming has great potential to show them that they can navigate these problems and move forward. A don't give up mindset.

Of course sloppy rubbish games that have no meaning to them bother me, but the growing trend of co-op games, like Split Fiction (completed with the 7 year old), Orbitals, even LEGO Batman, has a great way of channelling their gaming and being a chance to create some really great memories.

Now if Nintendo could just make an open world Zelda co-op that would be great.

A concern but not serious one for me is how to introduce gaming to them. Do I start with something like Mario 1 to not spoil (and probably overwhelm) them with graphics? What after that? I want them to appreciate the classics but don't want to overdo it and make them resent it instead. Just gotta play it by ear

#4065. Battlefield 6 is getting a free trial next week with a decent selection of maps and modes

Battlefield 6's second-ever free trial, and the first in 2026, is upon us.

Battlefield Studios has announced that Battlefield 6 is going free to play for one week next week. Well, a portion of the game is, anyway, as part of a free trial that will include some of the game’s most popular modes and maps.

Though it does not encompass the entirety of the game, the free trial is fairly generous. Here’s what to expect.

For starters, the trial kicks off Tuesday, March 17 and will run until the following Tuesday, March 24. The trial will be accessible from Battlefield Redsec, the already free-to-play portion of the game.

Once downloaded, you’ll find a new Battlefield 6 Free Trial section in the main menu. Because Redsec and Battlefield 6 multiplayer share progression, if you played the former at any point, you’ll be able to pick up from where you left off.

The same is also true the other way around; if this is your first time with Battlefield 6, all your unlocks will carry over to the full version, as well as to Redsec if you decide stick with the free-to-play off-shoot.

Once it kicks off, you’ll find three playlists to choose from. Casual Breakthrough, All-out Warfare, and a third playlist showcasing the new Nightfall game mode and its associated map.

All-out Warfare is what you come to Battlefield for, and that playlist features Conquest, Breakthrough, as well as BF6’s newcomer Escalation - all large-scale, combined arms game modes. They will be playable across four maps. You get to play on two from Season 2: Contaminated, and Hagental Base, one from Season 1: Eastwood, and Mirak Valley from the base game.

Casual Breakthrough is based on a playlist that already exists in the core game, and it’s really designed as a nice on-ramp for new players. It also offers less intense gameplay, perfect for people grinding unlocks.

Casual Breakthrough is limited to just 16 real players (eight per team), with the rest filled up with bots. You earn the same amount of XP in those matches, except when you interact with bots, so killing a bot will net less than a human player. Outside of that, unlocks, Challenges and all other things that don’t depend on stat-tracking can be done within.

In the trial, the Casual Breakthrough playlist includes Hagental Base, Contaminated, and Eastwood.

The most interesting is the third playlist, in part because its content will also be available to owners of the full game for the first time right alongside free-to-play players. Nightfall is a playlist exclusive to the Hagental Base map.

This is a very small map, so the mode selection here is Team Deathmatch, Squad Deathmatch, and Domination. Under Nightfall conditions, lights across the entire map are turned off, so you’re going to have use your NVGs to be able to see. This is also a god opportunity to try out weapon attachments that specifically work under low-light conditions, which typically don’t get much use in multiplayer.

March 17 also marks the launch of the second stage of Battlefield 6’s Season 2, which comes with the aforementioned Nightfall content, as well as a big new update - so the timing works out nicely for everyone.

The release of DOOM: The Dark Ages Revelations saw critics heaping praise on the expansion earlier in 2026, to the point where it's actually even in the Game of the Year (or at least Expansion of the Year) conversation as things stand.

"Complete rounds to earn Skulls, which unlock rewards such as Slaughter Mode-only Slayer skins, weapon skins for all modes and profile icons. Tear through relentless, escalating and unpredictable waves of demonic hordes, carving out your personal best scores and unlocking rewards using the Skulls collected from the carnage. #4063. GTA 6: The Big Review Round-Up

Sam Woods is TheGamer’s Senior Reporter. He’s been in games journalism since 2020 and has undertaken a variety of roles in that time. These have included roles such as SEO Editor, Managing Editor at DualShockers, and Global Head of Gaming, and he's also been seen on the BBC. He was promoted to the Senior Reporter position in 2025 following a series of high-quality reports and exclusives for TheGamer.

Since 2020, Sam has written over 3,000 articles and specializes in telling the stories of the people behind the games. He’s interviewed the biggest game directors, some of the industry’s top talents, told the stories of how indie games came to be, and spoken to players about what really makes them tick. He’s also interviewed some of the world’s biggest musical artists to find out how the medium has inspired their work, and TV and Film actors about their roles in video game adaptations. He even hosted a PAX panel in 2021 and made a documentary in 2024 surrounding the creation of a Disney game.

Alongside this, Sam focuses on breaking news. He got the scoop on Perfect Dark’s cancellation, provided context on some AI drama, and revealed that Lady Dimitrescu’s actress would love to step back into the character’s giant shoes. These articles have been picked up by the biggest gaming sites, including IGN, GameSpot, and PC Gamer. He also loves to dive into the numbers behind the games.

Sam’s journey in games journalism has taken him all over the world. He’s covered Gamescom in Germany, Summer Game Fest in Los Angeles, and Tokyo Game Show in Japan, each on three occasions.

He’s been learning Japanese since 2024 with the intention of identifying and translating Japanese-language news and bringing it to English-language audiences first, something he’s done countless times.

Sam’s first review was 2020’s Battletoads reboot, and he’s since reviewed games in The Legend of Zelda, Super Mario, and Pokemon franchises.

With less than 24 hours until Grand Theft Auto 6 launches, the game's review embargo has lifted, and it's everything we expected it would be. The game opened to a staggering 99 on both Metacritic and OpenCritic, making it officially the best-reviewed game of all time. If there were any doubts that Rockstar might fumble the bag, they have now been put to bed.

Its glowing reviews are best captured in quotes from critics around the world. We've trawled through these reviews and gathered them into a full round-up featuring the thoughts from some of the industry's most notable reviewers. Hopefully this will amp up your excitement another notch ahead of tonight's release.

We'll start off with our very own George Foster, who delivered an astounding 5/5 review. He called it the most "high-pressure thing" he's ever taken on, but it seems like it was worth it. The game constantly left him "speechless," and he says it sets "an impossible new bar for the medium," but his thoughts are perhaps best summarized in the comment below:

"Without a shadow of a doubt, Grand Theft Auto 6 is the best open-world game I’ve ever played, and one of the best games, full stop, with only incredibly minute nitpicks barely worth mentioning that do nothing to drag it down from masterpiece status."

Unsurprisingly, GameSpot's Tamoor Hussain also scored the game a 10/10. He said, "This game is the culmination of everything the developer has previously achieved in the open-world space that pushes the genre to heights that, in all likelihood, no other developer will be able to reach. GTA 6 is an astonishing open-world action game that I’d wager won’t be outdone until Grand Theft Auto 7."

Josh West had the honor of reviewing GTA 6 for GamesRadar+. They were seemingly just as blown away by the game as everybody else, saying, "With impossible production values, details that matter, and an interconnected set of world systems that bring this world to life, GTA VI is unlike anything we’ve ever seen. Jason and Lucia are the beating heart of this game, and the story they tell is worth living. This isn’t just a good game, or a great game, it’s the kind that comes just once a generation."

The 10s keep rolling in, with Luke Reilly giving it another perfect score for IGN. They said, "I was simply not ready for just how much richer, deeper, and more satisfying Grand Theft Auto 6 has proven to be. After three weeks and over 120 hours playing it, I’m still hopelessly hooked, absorbing the world at walking speed like a tourist in a new town. I’m dazed by just how consistently I find myself noticing a new animation, unique pedestrian, or standout vehicle. I am completely enamoured with its series-best car handling and weaving through the realistically dense traffic. Put simply, Grand Theft Auto 6 is the single most impressive video game I have ever played."

VGC's Jordan Middler said the game "does so much at such a high bar" in their 5/5 review. Like many of his fellow reviewers, Middler felt that it's a game that will likely never be matched. "This is Rockstar operating at the absolute peak of its power. The scale of Grand Theft Auto 6’s achievement won’t be felt this week, or next week, or even next year. It’ll be felt in the next decade of games that come after it, as developers, like so many before them, attempt to emulate the Rockstar magic. But nobody else can. No one has the budget, this number of developers, and this level of cultural impact."

One of the few 9/10 scores came from The New York Times and Yussef Cole. While not quite a 10, they were still enamored with the game, saying, "The surprising depth to which themes are explored makes for a memorable and endearing experience in Grand Theft Auto VI, which largely lives up to its sky-high expectations by inverting the series’s reputation for destruction."

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#4062. Honkai: Star Rail Version 4.1 livestream reveals a pared-back, four-week update as HoYo plays catch-up

Honkai: Star Rail will continue the Planarcadia story arc in Version 4.1, as the Star Rail Fest presents a new twist.

A new Honkai: Star Rail Special Program has concluded, which means some fresh news about the game’s upcoming major update. Version 4.1, unveiled today as Unraveled for Daybreak, is the action RPG’s next moment, kicking off on March 25.

Unraveled for Daybreak is the next chapter in the ongoing story of Planarcadia, with the Astra Express Crew now invited to a fan fest inspired by their own past journeys. The aptly named Star Rail Fest is ostensibly hosted to allow more of the citizens of Arcadia to experience the Trailblaze.

As everyone’s eyes is fixated on the grand Star Rail Fest, the Phantasmoon Games continue to be in full swing, as does the war with the Supplicants. Star Rail Fest is, however, the big focus of this update, in case it wasn't obvious.

The event is made up of three large-scale zones, each themed around past excursions of the Astral Express. You’ll get to explore the Belobog Zone, Xianzhou Luofu Zone, and Penacony Zone. Later on, you’ll also be able to visit Pearluxe Tower, the headquarters of Pearluxe Corp.

Each area will feature its own attractions, such as the balloon figures of Supreme Guardian Cocolia and the Destruction Engine, the duel against the Lord Ravager Phantylia at Scalegorge Waterscape, and the Pearluxe Tower’s Alloy King Pom-Pom model.

The hot new arrival is bumbling noirish detective Ashveil whom we've met in Version 4.0, and who becomes a playable character with this update. Ashveil is a 5-Star Lightning-Type character, on the Path of The Hunt. You’ll be able to pull for him throughout 4.1's runtime, which is slightly reduced at four weeks instead of the usual six, in order to rebalance the schedule after the extra-long Version 3.8.

In combat, Ashveil is capable of increasing Crit Damage of all allies. He can also mark an enemy as Bait, which reduces the Defence of all enemies on the field so long as this tag holds. If Ashveil uses his Skill on the baited target, he will deal extra Damage and regain Skill Points for the team.

Ashveil can bully that baited target even further by launching Hounding Pursuit. If any of his teammates attacks the Bait, he can further deliver a follow-up attack that gradually accumulates Gluttony for as long as he’s in combat. Gluttony can later be consumed to boost follow-up attack damage.

If he lands a kill, Ashveil continues to deal damage to the next enemy he attacks. That buff is transferred if that enemy is killed. Even in map exploration, Ashveil can be deadly, capable of inflicting Stunned upon enemies within a specific range.

Returning characters this patch will be Hyacine in the first half, and Boothill in the second half. Once again, due to the reduced runtime, their banner reruns will be slightly shorter than normal, at just two weeks each instead of three — so be sure to take that into account if you're planning on pulling for either of them.

Version 4.1 also adds the Wispae War Saga, a new activity where you can practice your leadership skills by commanding different types of Wispae Soldiers in the Graphia Academy. You can upgrade each one, use spell cards to alter their effects, and later face other champions. You ultimately want to play this to unlock new Wispae Companions, not to mention complete the challenges within.

Finally, Version 4.1 marks the start of a new Arcadian Chronicles phase in the Divergent Universe. You’ll be able to use Waypoint Pass cards to explore the different areas. HoYo is also bringing back Planar Fissure and Garden of Plenty with double rewards. And as ever, if you log in for at least seven days after downloading the new patch, you’ll earn 10 premium banner pulls.

In 2008, Kojima Productions released what was billed as the swan song for Hideo Kojima's Metal Gear series: Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots. The game had the staggering task of tying up decades of storytelling by bringing together Solid Snake, Ocelot, Otacon, Raiden, and many more characters for one explosive finale. The adventure centers on a rapidly aging Solid Snake racing against the clock to stop his twin and nemesis, Liquid Snake, one last time. Of course, there are far more bizarre shenanigans at play.

Guns of the Patriots was acclaimed for its storytelling, cinematic presentation, and evolution of the series' stealth gameplay, namely the OctoCamo suit that allowed Snake to mimic the appearance/texture of any surface he touched. #4060. Zenless Zone Zero Version 2.7 brings Angels of Delusion to the battlefield with playable Nangong Yu

Champions Never Fall to the Past indeed, as Zenless Zone Zero prepares for a major update that fans of Angels of Delusion will appreciate.

HoYoverse has delivered another Special Program for the second day running, this time for Zenless Zone Zero. The developer revealed the full details of Version 2.7, subtitled Champions Never Fall to the Past.

This next major update arrives March 24, adding two new Agents, and introducing the Hollow Champion competition.

Most things in Version 2.7 follow on from the Hollow Champion competition, which brings together old friends and familiar faces, as well interesting newcomers. Everyone is in it to win some big rewards and earn glory.

Among the unexpected participants the competition has attracted are the Public Security's Metropolitan Order Division, and even some former Calydon's Sweepers. A big challenge that awaits is Black Wolf Romeul, who’s capable of increasing his Crit Damage Resistance and Interruption Resistance by activating a Corruptive Barrier.

Romeul can also cause enemies to continuously lose HP, but you can beat him by putting together a squad that can deal sustained Anomaly damage, which will break through the barrier quickly.

Our first new arrival in Version 2.7 is Cissia of the Metropolitan Order Division. She is an S-Rank Electric Attack Agent who automatically gains three stacks of Venom when she enters the battle. Each stack deals Electric Damage while also increasing her Crit Rate for a time.

When she runs out of Venom, which will happen, Cissia can generate more stacks by using her EX Special Attack. She can also use her Basic Attack, Serpent's Kiss, to better utilise the new stacks of Venom she generates.

The other new Agent may be the more exciting. Nangong Yu, the captain and lead dancer of the Angels of Delusion, can now be part of your team. Nangong Yu is an S-Rank Ether Stun Agent who can boost her team’s Anomaly Buildup Rate against Stunned enemies.

Being part of an idol group has its perks, because she automatically regenerates Downbeat as time goes on, and even more any time a squad member inflicts an enemy with Anomaly. Nangong Yu can then use Downbeat - after enough has been accumulated - on charged attacks that keep enemies stunned for longer. Her Ultimate triggers Ether Veil: Delusion Reprise, which boosts the entire squad’s Attack.

Returning Agents in Version 2.7 will be Yidhari, the S-Rank Ice Rupture Agent, as well as Seed, the Electric Attack Agent.

Outside of all the very important action in the core story, this chapter also brings new themed events to Lumina Square’s Simmer Hot Pot Restaurant. The Simulated Battle Trial is also getting some love, with updated mechanics and new enemy line-ups.

Catch up on our recently updated Zenless Zone Zero character tier list, and don’t forget to check out these Zenless Zone Zero codes before you jump in for some free stuff.
